items.item: Copying to remote and deleting from local are two separate events gated by two separate conditions, not one event under two names.

items.item: A segment can be simultaneously present in both the local and remote tiers for a while — that overlap is the normal, expected state while local retention is still running out.

items.item: The fetch API's uniformity is a deliberate design choice, not an accident — it's what lets tiered storage be adopted without any consumer-side code change.

at.step: Reveal: transparent, but not free

items.item: Shrinking local retention aggressively while total retention stays long doesn't save storage cost overall — it just shifts more of the same data into the remote tier sooner.

at.step: Reveal: two retention knobs, not one

items.item: The compacted-topics restriction is a direct consequence of what compaction does to a segment's bytes (topic 6), not an arbitrary product limitation layered on top.

items.item: This topic's cost framing and topic 6's retention framing are the same mechanism viewed from two angles: where bytes live, versus how long they're kept at all.

items.item: The ordering guarantees from the previous topic are completely undisturbed by tiering — moving a segment's physical bytes never touches the sequence of records inside it.

items.item: A backfill or disaster-recovery job that reads a wide historical range should expect its latency profile to differ sharply from a normal tail-read workload, precisely because of this cold-read cost.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Fully leaderless, diskless designs remove the local tier from the hot path entirely rather than layering a remote tier on top of it — a more radical version of the same cost pressure this topic addresses.
This topic closes out the chapter's log-mechanics arc (segments, replication, consumer groups, retention, ordering, tiering) before the next arc turns to correctness under failure.
